# Plot 
# Hint - use the .plot() method for Pandas Series, make sure all presidents show up on x-axis
plt.figure(figsize=(20,7))
counts.plot(kind="bar")
plt.title("Number of Speeches per President")
plt.xlabel("President")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
plt.savefig("outputs/speeches_per_president.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

The plot shows how many State of the Union speeches each president gave, ordered from the newest presidents on the left to the earliest presidents on the right. You can see a clear pattern where most presidents give around three to eight speeches, which makes sense because one term is four years and two terms is eight. Some presidents, like Franklin D. Roosevelt, gave many more because he served four terms. Early presidents like George Washington also have high counts since the format of the speech was different at the time. Recent presidents like Biden and Trump have fewer speeches simply because their time in office is shorter so far. Overall, the plot reflects both presidential term length and historical differences in how the SOTU was delivered.
Number of Speeches per Year

# Hint - Use value counts and sort by years
speeches_per_year = sou['Year'].value_counts().sort_index()
speeches_per_year

plt.figure(figsize=(12,5))
speeches_per_year.plot(kind='line')
plt.title("Number of Speeches per Year")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.savefig("outputs/speeches_per_year.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

The number of speeches per year is mostly one per year through almost the whole timeline. The only exceptions happen in the early years, where a few years have two or more speeches, and again around the mid twentieth century, where some presidents gave two in a single year. After that, it settles back to one per year. The pattern is basically flat, showing that the yearly speech tradition has stayed consistent, with only a few rare spikes.
Word Count Distribution

# Hint - try seaborn.histplot()
plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
sns.histplot(sou['Word Count'], bins=18, kde=False, color='steelblue')
plt.title('Distribution of State of the Union Speech Word Counts')
plt.xlabel('Word Count')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.savefig("outputs/distribution_of_state_of_the_union_speech_word_counts", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

The distribution of word counts is very skewed. Most State of the Union speeches fall between about three thousand and eight thousand words, which shows that presidents usually stay within a similar range. After that, the counts drop off quickly and only a few speeches go above ten thousand words. The long tail on the right comes from unusually long speeches, but those are rare. Overall, the plot shows that shorter speeches are much more common, and extremely long ones are outliers.
Word Count Distribution over Year

# Hint: try seaborn.rugplot()
plt.figure()
sns.scatterplot(data=sou, x='Word Count', y='Year')
sns.rugplot(data=sou, x='Word Count', y='Year')
plt.title("Speech Year Versus Word Count")
plt.savefig("outputs/speech_year_versus_word_count.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

The scatter plot shows that word counts have always been pretty spread out, but there is a clear shift over time. Early speeches in the late seventeen hundreds and early eighteen hundreds were shorter, usually under ten thousand words. As we move into the eighteen hundreds and mid nineteen hundreds, the range gets wider and a few presidents start giving much longer speeches. In the modern era, most speeches stay in the shorter range again, even though the overall pattern is still scattered. There is no strong linear trend, but the clusters by time period make it clear that different eras had different speaking habits.

Now, you should be good to go!
Some important definitions:
Token
: a single word or piece of a word
Lemma
: the core component of a word, e.g., “complete” is the lemma for “completed” and “completely”
Stop Word
: a common word that does not add semantic value, such as “a”, “and”, “the”, etc.
Vectorization
: representing a document as a vector where each index in the vector corresponds to a token or word and each entry is the count.
In this section, we will explore the most common tokens and lemmas throughout different slices of the speech data. We will also develop vectorization representations of the speeches.
